analysis.one_liner: Rolls back endangered species and river restoration rules to send more federal water to California farm districts.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 229-191 on February 5, 2014, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules governing the federal Central Valley Project, which delivers California river water largely to farms. It would order the two big federal and state water projects to be run under a 1994 agreement "without regard to the Endangered Species Act" [S3], cancel the San Joaquin River restoration settlement that reintroduces salmon [S3], guarantee minimum water deliveries to Sacramento Valley farm districts [S3], and let irrigation districts buy out their remaining federal construction debt at a discounted Treasury rate while dropping pricing and acreage limits [S3]. It also shortens a protected stretch of the Merced River [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Agricultural water contractors in California's Central Valley gain the most: guaranteed delivery percentages even in dry years (100% in wet-to-below-normal years, 75% in dry years) [S4], 40-year contract renewals instead of 25 [S3], the option to pay off remaining federal construction debt at a discounted Treasury rate with full-cost pricing and acreage limits no longer applying [S4], and an end to Endangered Species Act limits on project operations [S3]. Irrigation districts like Oakdale and South San Joaquin also win rights to store up to 300,000 acre-feet of their own water in New Melones Reservoir [S4]. A small community benefit is included: Kettleman City would get a contract for up to 900 acre-feet of municipal water [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees Sacramento Valley agricultural contractors at least 100% of contract quantities in wet, above-normal, and below-normal years, 75% in dry years, and 50% in critically dry years, insulating farms from drought-driven cuts.
Directs the Interior Secretary to renew CVP water contracts for 40 years instead of 25, and to charge only for water actually delivered, locking in long-term supply for irrigation districts.

Lets contractors convert long-term CVP contracts to repay remaining construction costs at a discounted Treasury rate, after which federal full-cost pricing and acreage limitations no longer apply to their lands — a large financial concession to water districts.

Orders the Central Valley Project and State Water Project to operate under the 1994 Bay-Delta Accord standards without regard to the Endangered Species Act or any other law governing their operation, removing the pumping restrictions that during the 2014 drought reduced farm deliveries.

Repeals the court-settled San Joaquin River restoration program, including the reintroduction of spring-run Chinook salmon, and orders restoration flows kept above Mendota Pool rather than flowing downstream, freeing Friant Division water for its contractors.
Speeds up water transfers by requiring agencies to rule on transfer proposals within 45 days and barring the Secretary from imposing mitigation requirements on them.
Adds Kettleman City as an authorized CVP service area with a contract for up to 900 acre-feet of municipal and industrial water, a modest benefit for a disadvantaged valley town.

analysis.who_pays: The San Joaquin River's salmon runs and the people who depend on them — the bill repeals the reintroduction of spring-run Chinook salmon and the restoration settlement worked out in federal court [S3]. Commercial and recreational salmon fishermen would face reduced fish runs. Federal taxpayers would absorb a discounted buyout of irrigation districts' remaining construction debt and the loss of full-cost pricing requirements [S4]. The state of California would lose authority: the bill preempts state restrictions on water rights for species protection and on the public trust doctrine, and waives federal environmental review by deeming state CEQA filings sufficient under NEPA [S4]. Tribes and downstream communities that relied on the settlement's claims process and flows would lose their negotiated remedies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fisheries, taxpayers, and state water authority

drawbacks.text: Repealing the San Joaquin River settlement reneges on a legal settlement the federal government agreed to in court with conservation groups and Friant farmers, which had exchanged restoration flows for the farmers' release from liability — undermining the reliability of any future negotiated water settlement.

Counting hatchery-spawned fish the same as wild-spawned fish in Endangered Species Act determinations can mask the true decline of wild salmon runs, risking listings decisions that no longer reflect whether wild populations can survive on their own.

The bill deems state environmental filings sufficient to meet NEPA and exempts the Stanislaus River predator-removal pilot from NEPA entirely, removing federal environmental review of major project actions.

An honest supporter would acknowledge the 2014 drought emergency was real — the Governor had declared one on January 17, 2014, which the bill explicitly preserves [S4] — but the bill went far beyond emergency relief, permanently rewriting contracts, discounting construction debt buyouts, and repealing a restoration program rather than providing temporary drought water.

Suspending non-mandatory fish and wildlife restoration whenever CVP delivery capability falls short of an 800,000 acre-foot increase target ties environmental recovery directly to water deliveries, so in dry times the environment absorbs the shortfall.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Drought relief for San Joaquin Valley farms and communities was a genuine need, and the Kettleman City water contract is a real if small benefit. But the bill's core is a structural rewrite that permanently shifts federally subsidized water toward large irrigation districts: guaranteed deliveries in dry years, discounted debt buyouts, waived environmental review, and Endangered Species Act carve-outs, paid for by salmon runs, fishing communities, tribes, and the federal treasury. A narrower drought-relief measure could have addressed the emergency without repealing a court settlement or locking in the contract and debt terms, which is why even supporters of valley water faced a steep cost-benefit trade.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in February 2014, but the Senate left it sitting on its calendar, never debated or voted, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative David Valadao introduced the bill on January 29, 2014, during California's severe drought, and it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee.

The House Rules Committee brought it straight to the floor under a rule that allowed only pre-printed amendments; eight Democratic amendments to modify it were all rejected, most on voice votes before recorded votes could be counted.

On February 5, 2014, a motion to recommit — a last chance to send the bill back to committee with instructions to add protections for local water supplies and tribal sovereignty — failed 191-231, with 226 of 231 Republicans voting no.
The House passed the bill 229-191, with 222 of 231 Republicans in favor and only 7 of 200 Democrats crossing over.

The Senate received the bill on February 6 and placed it on its legislative calendar on February 10, 2014; no committee acted, no vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, San Joaquin River salmon restoration and its reintroduction of spring-run Chinook salmon remained in place, the Endangered Species Act continued to apply to Central Valley Project operations, and taxpayers did not fund the discounted debt buyouts. Central Valley farm districts stayed under the existing legal regime — with its drought-driven delivery cuts — rather than gaining the guaranteed supplies the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Salmon, tribes, and existing water law

sides.party_line_note: The vote split sharply by party: 222 of 231 Republicans voted yes while only 7 of 200 Democrats did, and the motion to recommit failed with zero Republican support (226 of 231 voting no).

industries.industry: Central Valley agricultural water contractors and irrigation districts
industries.note: The bill guarantees them minimum deliveries even in dry years, extends contracts to 40 years, lets them buy out remaining federal construction debt at a discount, and lifts Endangered Species Act limits on the pumps and reservoirs that serve them. Their gain comes directly from water formerly directed to fish, river restoration, and environmental compliance.

The bill repeals the San Joaquin River settlement that reintroduces spring-run Chinook salmon and orders project operations to proceed without regard to the Endangered Species Act, shrinking the salmon runs the industry depends on. Healthy fisheries are a public resource, so the industry's loss tracks the public's.

The debt-conversion title lets irrigation districts retire their remaining Central Valley Project construction repayment obligations at a discounted Treasury rate and then escape federal full-cost pricing and acreage limits, shifting the cost of federally built water infrastructure away from its beneficiaries.
